title: Group Purchasing Organizations
one_liner: GPOs aggregate member purchasing volume to negotiate lower prices and better terms, with healthcare remaining the dominant U.S. market.
overview: Group purchasing organizations negotiate vendor contracts on behalf of member buyers rather than taking title to goods. Healthcare GPOs remain the core of the industry because hospitals and non-acute providers rely on them for medical-surgical supplies, pharmaceuticals, capital equipment, food, facilities, IT and purchased services. The model has expanded beyond healthcare into government, education, nonprofits, corporate indirect spend, private equity portfolios and real estate. Industry demand in 2025-2026 is being pulled by hospital margin pressure, elevated supply and drug inflation, tariff uncertainty, persistent shortages and the need for better data, contract compliance and supply-chain resilience. Competition is rising from large health systems that self-contract, regional alliances, e-procurement platforms and broader cooperative purchasing networks.

key_stats.market_size: $7.3 billion in U.S. industry revenue in 2025
key_stats.healthcare_adoption: More than 95% of U.S. hospitals use GPOs, 2024-2025 referenced industry estimate
key_stats.gpo_savings: Up to $55 billion in annual U.S. healthcare cost savings attributed to GPOs in HSCA-cited research, 2025
key_stats.hospital_cost_pressure: U.S. hospital total expenses grew 7.5% in 2025, while supplies grew 9.9% and drugs grew 13.6%
key_stats.premier_2025_revenue: Premier reported $1.013 billion in fiscal 2025 net revenue; supply-chain net administrative fees were $556.3 million in fiscal 2025
key_stats.vizient_scale: Vizient reported $168 billion in annual purchasing volume and reach across 69% of U.S. acute-care hospitals in 2025-2026 website disclosures

baseline_2022.market_size: About $5.1 billion in 2022 baseline revenue, extrapolated from the source file's 2021 $5.0 billion revenue and 2021-2027 1.17% projected CAGR
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 6.1% in 2021 baseline profit margin, used as the closest baseline margin indicator
baseline_2022.healthcare_share: More than 60.0% of industry revenue from healthcare in the 2021 baseline
baseline_2022.establishments: 731 establishments in 2021 baseline, with 1.51% projected CAGR from 2021 to 2027

how_it_makes_money: GPOs primarily earn vendor-paid administrative fees tied to member purchases under negotiated contracts, commonly around 1% to 3% of purchase price in healthcare contracts. They also earn revenue from member services, supplier programs, software, analytics, procurement technology, consulting, supply-chain co-management, procure-to-pay services, private-label or direct sourcing programs and category-specific advisory work.
cost_structure: The largest costs are skilled procurement, contracting, clinical category management, analytics, compliance and member-service labor; technology platforms and data infrastructure; sales and account management; legal and regulatory compliance; supplier-relations operations; and revenue-share payments or fee rebates to members. GPOs are not usually inventory-heavy because they generally do not take title to contracted goods, although some have added direct sourcing, resiliency and distribution-adjacent capabilities that can raise working-capital and operational complexity.
current_dynamics: The industry is benefiting from buyers' renewed focus on expense control in 2025-2026. Hospitals face rising labor, supply, drug, tariff and administrative costs, making GPO savings, standardization and purchased-services optimization more valuable. At the same time, larger integrated delivery networks are negotiating harder over fee shares, demanding more transparency and selectively self-contracting where they have enough scale. GPOs are responding by adding AI-enabled analytics, spend visibility, e-procurement, supplier-risk monitoring, clinical value analysis and advisory services. Non-healthcare cooperative purchasing is also gaining traction as education, government, nonprofit and enterprise buyers look for faster compliant purchasing and indirect-spend savings.
whats_growing: Spend analytics, contract-compliance tools, pharmacy sourcing, purchased-services contracting, capital equipment advisory, private-label and domestic sourcing, non-acute healthcare purchasing, public-sector cooperative contracts, corporate indirect-spend programs and AI-assisted supply-chain decision support are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Pure commodity contract access without analytics or service support is becoming less differentiated. Standalone third-party GPO value is under pressure where large health systems self-contract, consolidate suppliers or demand higher administrative-fee sharebacks. Premier's fiscal 2025 supply-chain net administrative-fee revenue fell 11% from fiscal 2024, showing fee-share and member-renewal pressure at major healthcare GPOs.
recent_developments: Apr 2025: AHA's 2025 Cost of Caring report said U.S. hospital expenses grew 7.5% in 2025, supplies 9.9% and drugs 13.6%, reinforcing GPO demand for cost containment.

Jul 2025: Journal of Public Economics published evidence that greater GPO scale reduced average hospital supply expenses by 2.7%, equal to about $48 per discharge and $0.72 million annually per hospital.
Aug 2025: Premier's fiscal 2025 10-K reported $1.013 billion in net revenue and an 11% decline in net administrative-fee revenue due mainly to higher member fee share under renewed GPO contracts.
Sep 2025: Premier agreed to be acquired by Patient Square Capital in a $2.6 billion take-private transaction.
Nov 2025: Premier closed the Patient Square Capital acquisition and stopped trading on Nasdaq.
Feb 2026: HealthTrust promoted Jocelyn Bradshaw to President of GPO Operations, citing inflation, supply disruption and tariff challenges as priorities for GPO execution.
outlook: Industry revenue should keep expanding modestly through 2026 as cost pressure, hospital consolidation, non-acute care growth and indirect-spend programs increase reliance on aggregated purchasing. The strongest GPOs will be those that combine scale with analytics, clinical standardization, supply-risk visibility and execution support. Margin pressure will persist because large members are renegotiating fee shares, suppliers are scrutinizing access costs and health systems can self-contract in selected categories. Regulatory and antitrust scrutiny around vendor fees, transparency, exclusivity and competition remains a standing risk, but the economic case for GPO participation is stronger when hospitals face high supply, drug and tariff-related inflation.
one_sentence: The U.S. group purchasing organization industry is a scale-driven procurement-services market where hospitals, health systems, public agencies, schools, nonprofits and enterprises use collective buying power to reduce supply, drug, equipment and purchased-services costs.

title: Gun & Ammunition Stores
one_liner: Specialty firearms retailers remain a large but fragmented retail market, with 2025 demand below pandemic/election peaks and 2026 checks showing renewed year-over-year growth.
overview: The industry consists of specialty retailers that primarily sell guns and ammunition, often supplemented by accessories, optics, storage products, gunsmithing, training, range relationships and transfer services. The baseline IBIS file described 2021 revenue of $15.0 billion after a pandemic-era demand spike, projected 2026 revenue of $17.0 billion, low concentration, low capital intensity, heavy regulation and high external competition. Current public market references indicate a larger post-2021 retail base: IBIS-cited third-party summaries put 2024 gun retail revenue at $23.1 billion and 2026 gun and ammunition stores market size at about $23.5 billion, while GrabAGun's 2025 SEC filing cited a possible $25.0 billion 2024 U.S. retail addressable market for firearms, ammunition and related accessories. Demand is no longer at 2020-2021 surge levels: annual 2025 NSSF-adjusted NICS checks were 14.612 million, down 4.1% from 2024, but monthly 2026 adjusted checks turned positive through June 2026, including 1.123 million in June 2026, up 11.7% year over year.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: about $23.5 billion U.S. gun and ammunition stores revenue, based on IBIS-cited public summaries; 2024: $23.1 billion gun retail revenue cited by Gitnux from IBISWorld; 2024: up to $25.0 billion U.S. retail addressable market cited by GrabAGun SEC filing.

key_stats.businesses: 2026: about 23,019 U.S. gun and ammunition store businesses, based on IBIS-cited public summary; 2025: 16,396 businesses and 118,697 employees were cited for 2022 in the startup-guide summary of IBIS data.
key_stats.demand_indicator: 2025: 14,612,314 NSSF-adjusted NICS checks versus 15,239,011 in 2024; Q4 2025 adjusted checks were 4,294,591, down 3.7% from Q4 2024.
key_stats.retail_footprint: 2025: ATF-linked summaries reported about 46,072 Type 01 dealer FFLs in FY 2025; 2026: third-party ATF-based directories reported roughly 45,500 active Type 01 dealers and about 76,500 active FFLs across all license types.
key_stats.economic_context: 2024: NSSF estimated the broader firearm and ammunition industry's total U.S. economic impact at $91.7 billion, up from $90.5 billion in 2023, supporting nearly 383,000 full-time-equivalent jobs.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: approximately $19.6 billion, inferred from the public IBIS-cited statement that the industry was worth $20.0 billion in 2023 with projected 2023 growth of 1.9%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: 1.8% market-size growth, cited in the public IBISWorld link excerpt reproduced by Step By Step Business.
baseline_2022.businesses: 2022: 16,396 gun and ammunition store businesses, cited from IBISWorld by Step By Step Business.
baseline_2022.employment: 2022: 118,697 employees, cited from IBISWorld by Step By Step Business.
baseline_2022.baseline_file_context: 2021 baseline file: $15.0 billion revenue, 7.2% 2021 growth, 5.0% EBIT margin, 8,932 establishments, 101,239 employees and projected 2026 revenue of $17.0 billion in 2021 dollars.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue from firearm sales, ammunition sales, firearm accessories, optics, magazines, safes, cleaning supplies, holsters, hunting and shooting apparel, gunsmithing, training, transfer fees, special orders, consignment, memberships, layaway/financing and online-to-FFL pickup transactions. Ammunition and accessories are recurring, higher-frequency purchases, while firearms are more cyclical and sensitive to regulatory expectations, promotional pricing and consumer confidence.
cost_structure: The largest cost is merchandise purchases from manufacturers, wholesalers and distributors. Labor is material because compliance, customer education, fitting, repair intake and safe handling require knowledgeable staff. Other costs include rent, insurance, security systems, payment processing, shipping, inventory financing, shrink prevention, ATF/state compliance, background-check workflow, e-commerce systems, marketing and professional services. The baseline IBIS file reported 2021 EBIT margin of about 5.0%, with profitability helped by shortage-era pricing but pressured by online merchants, pawn shops, sporting goods stores, private sales and normalization of supply.
major_players: Local independent FFL dealers and specialty gun shops
current_dynamics: The market is fragmented and regulation-heavy, with specialty retailers competing against sporting-goods chains, pawn shops, gun shows, online marketplaces and private-sale channels. 2025 was softer than 2024 by the main purchase-related background-check proxy, but 2026 monthly adjusted NICS through June showed year-over-year gains after several years of normalization from 2020-2021 peaks. Regulatory uncertainty remains a demand catalyst and an operating cost driver: ATF's 2024 dealer-definition final rule, 2025 Supreme Court ghost-gun decision, state merchant-category-code requirements and 2026 ATF deregulatory proposals all affect compliance planning, payment processing and online/storefront strategy.
whats_growing: Omnichannel firearms retail with online browsing, local FFL pickup and networked dealer fulfillment.
Recurring ammunition, bulk ammunition, optics, safes, parts, magazines and accessories that lift basket size beyond firearm unit sales.
Compliance-enabled e-commerce platforms; GrabAGun cited more than 78,000 products and a nationwide network of about 42,000 FFL dealers in 2025 SEC materials.
Younger and mobile-first buyers; GrabAGun cited roughly 60% mobile transaction mix for the 12 months ended October 2024.
2026 purchase-related background-check momentum, with adjusted NICS up year over year from February through June 2026 in public NSSF/SGB reports.
whats_shrinking: Pandemic-era scarcity premiums and panic-buying intensity have faded versus 2020-2021 peaks.
2025 annual NSSF-adjusted NICS checks declined 4.1% from 2024, signaling softer firearm unit demand for many retailers.
Large general retailers' firearms exposure remains reduced after Walmart, Dick's Sporting Goods and Amazon restrictions noted in SEC risk disclosures.
Independent stores face margin pressure from price-transparent online sellers, marketplace fulfillment, high insurance/compliance costs and inventory carrying costs.
Unadjusted FBI NICS checks in several 2026 months were still down year over year even when adjusted purchase-related checks rose, reflecting fewer permit/recheck transactions.
recent_developments: 2024-04-10: ATF signed the final rule redefining when sellers are 'engaged in the business' as firearms dealers, with a May 2024 effective date and later litigation limits.
2025-03-26: The U.S. Supreme Court decided Bondi v. Vanderstok, upholding ATF treatment of certain weapon-parts kits and unfinished frames or receivers under Gun Control Act requirements.
2025-05-01: California, Colorado and New York merchant-acquirer requirements for firearms merchant category code MCC 5723 took effect according to Bank of America merchant guidance.
2026-01-07: NSSF reported 2025 annual adjusted NICS checks of 14,612,314, down 4.1% from 15,239,011 in 2024.
2026-05-06: ATF proposed revising the 2024 'engaged in the business' dealer rule, with comments open through August 4, 2026.
2026-07-02: NSSF/SGB reported June 2026 adjusted NICS checks of 1,123,006, up 11.7% from June 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is mixed but healthier than the 2025 annual decline suggests. Retail revenue is supported by a large installed base of gun owners, recurring ammunition demand, accessories, training, storage and e-commerce-enabled FFL transfer networks. Firearm unit growth is likely to remain cyclical: election and regulation concerns can pull demand forward, while lower perceived regulatory urgency, inflation and normalized inventories can soften traffic. Stores with inventory discipline, strong compliance operations, online discovery, local expertise and accessory/service attachment should outperform pure transactional retailers. Key risks are regulatory reversals, state-level sales restrictions, payment-processing complexity, insurer and bank risk appetite, online price competition and demand volatility tied to political events.

title: Guns & Ammunition Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A volatile defense-and-consumer manufacturing industry where 2025 revenue is supported by munitions demand, allied rearmament, and resilient but softer civilian firearm demand.
overview: The industry spans civilian firearm brands, small-caliber ammunition plants, and large defense contractors producing ammunition, artillery and related ordnance. In the 2022 IBISWorld baseline, revenue was $21.108 billion, after 2020 revenue surged 21.6% and 2022 revenue slipped 0.4%. By 2025, public market references place the US guns and ammunition manufacturing market near $23.5 billion, implying roughly 3.6% annualized growth from 2022 to 2025. Demand is split between a choppy civilian channel, where 2024 domestic firearm production reached 9.475 million units and 2025 retail firearm unit sales weakened, and a strengthening defense channel, where FY2025 and FY2026 budgets emphasize munitions, missile defense, stockpile replenishment and defense industrial base capacity.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $23.5 billion in US industry revenue
key_stats.growth: 2022-2025: about 3.6% CAGR, based on $21.108 billion in 2022 and about $23.5 billion in 2025
key_stats.civilian_background_checks: 2024: 15,239,011 NSSF-adjusted checks for retail firearm sales, down 3.5% from 2023; 2025: about 14.6 million adjusted checks cited by NSSF
key_stats.defense_budget_signal: FY2025: $29.8 billion requested for munitions; FY2026: $838.7 billion discretionary defense appropriations bill approved with an additional $3.0 billion for munitions production and R&D
key_stats.baseline_profitability: 2022: $3.441 billion profit and 16.3% profit margin in the IBISWorld baseline

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: small arms and machine guns 38.5%, small arms ammunition 32.1%, other ammunition 23.7%, ordnance and accessories 5.7%

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue from selling civilian pistols, rifles, shotguns, parts and ammunition through distributors and retailers; from ammunition and ordnance contracts with the Department of Defense, law enforcement and allied governments; and from exports. In 2022, small arms and machine guns generated 38.5% of revenue, small arms ammunition 32.1%, other ammunition 23.7%, and ordnance/accessories 5.7%. In FY2026, demand is reinforced by federal procurement and R&D funding for weapon systems, munitions and missile-defense replenishment.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline shows profit at 16.3% of revenue and wages at $3.798 billion, or about 18.0% of 2022 revenue. The remaining 2022 cost base was dominated by metal inputs, explosives and propellants, components, energy, compliance, depreciation, contract engineering and distribution. Purchases are sensitive to 2025-2026 copper, steel, brass, nitrocellulose, propellant and energetic-material supply conditions, while large defense contractors can offset labor pressure with automation and long-cycle contracts.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Civilian firearm demand has cooled from pandemic-era peaks, with 2024 adjusted background checks down 3.5% from 2023 and 2025 same-store new firearm unit sales down about 13% from 2024 in Gearfire data. Defense demand is stronger: the FY2025 budget request included $29.8 billion for munitions, while FY2026 appropriations added munitions procurement authority and $3.0 billion for munitions production and R&D. Ammunition producers benefit from continued shooting-sports participation, law-enforcement replenishment and allied demand, but face raw-material, energetic-material and capacity constraints.
whats_growing: Defense munitions, missile-defense interceptors, artillery ammunition, ammunition capacity expansion, suppressors and NFA-related accessories are growing in 2025-2026. FY2026 appropriations added $2.1 billion above request for selected missile-defense quantities and $650 million for solid-rocket-motor capacity, while January 2026 ATF e-Forms activity reportedly jumped to about 150,000 filings on January 1, 2026 after the federal tax on suppressors, short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns fell to $0.
whats_shrinking: Civilian firearm unit demand is shrinking from the 2020-2022 surge. US firearm production fell from 2022 to 2023 and was 9,474,540 units in 2024, still below 2022 levels. NSSF-adjusted retail background checks fell 3.5% in 2024 versus 2023, and 2025 same-store new firearm unit sales were reported down about 13% from 2024. Entry-level firearm makers, distributors and retailers tied to discretionary civilian demand face more discounting and inventory pressure than defense-oriented ammunition and ordnance suppliers.
recent_developments: 2024-11-27: CSG completed its acquisition of The Kinetic Group, adding Federal, Remington, CCI, Speer, Hevi-Shot and Alliant Powder, with FY2024 Kinetic revenue of $1.5 billion.
2025-06-26: DoD outlined a FY2026 national defense budget request of $1.01 trillion, including $113.3 billion in mandatory funding and priorities for munitions production.
2026-01-15: NSSF reported 2023 AFMER domestic firearm production of 8,466,729 units, down 15.4% from 2022.
2026-02-03: Congress approved the FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act with $838.7 billion in discretionary funding and an additional $3.0 billion for munitions production and R&D.
2026-02-23: Gearfire reported 2025 same-store new firearm unit sales declined about 13% from 2024 levels.
2026-06-19: Gearfire, citing 2024 ATF AFMER, reported 9,474,540 US firearms produced in 2024, down 3.0% from 2023.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is modestly positive but uneven. Defense ammunition and ordnance suppliers should benefit from US stockpile replenishment, allied rearmament, missile-defense spending and industrial-base capacity funding. Civilian small-arms demand should remain above pre-2020 levels but below pandemic peaks, with 2025 retail softness likely pressuring margins for manufacturers exposed to discretionary handguns and rifles. A reasonable base case is low- to mid-single-digit annual revenue growth after 2025, with upside from geopolitical escalation or new federal procurement and downside from tighter state regulation, weaker consumer spending or input shortages.

2024-2026 consolidation and foreign ownership in ammunition
2025-2026 exports to allies and security partners
one_sentence: Guns & Ammunition Manufacturing in the US makes small arms, ammunition, artillery, ordnance and accessories for civilians, law enforcement, the US military and allied governments, with 2025 market size estimated at about $23.5 billion after the 2020-2022 demand spike normalized.

title: Gym & Exercise Equipment Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A small US manufacturing base serves a much larger fitness-equipment market dominated by imported hardware, with growth tied to commercial gym refurbishments, connected equipment and strength-training demand.
overview: This industry manufactures treadmills, exercise bikes, ellipticals, weight-training systems, benches, free weights and connected fitness hardware for gyms, studios, schools, hotels, corporate wellness sites, government buyers and households. The 2022 baseline was $2.082 billion of US manufacturing revenue, and applying the 2022-2028 IBISWorld projected CAGR of about 2.5% implies roughly $2.24 billion in 2025 and $2.30 billion in 2026. Demand conditions are healthier than the pandemic unwind: US fitness facility membership reached 77 million in 2024 and 81 million in 2025, while 2025 HFA benchmarking showed 2024 median facility revenue growth of 9.9% and net membership growth of 5.5%. The constraint is that the US market buys far more equipment than US factories produce: the 2022 baseline had $6.099 billion of imports and 80.7% import share of domestic demand, reflecting Asian sourcing, private-label equipment and offshore production by US-branded companies.

how_it_makes_money: 2025 revenue comes from selling cardio machines, strength systems, free weights, benches, racks and connected fitness equipment to commercial facilities, institutional buyers, retailers, distributors and households.
2025 commercial sales include direct equipment packages, replacement cycles, service contracts, installation, financing support and facility-management software integrations.

2025 consumer sales are more exposed to online retail, sporting-goods stores and branded direct-to-consumer channels, especially for bikes, treadmills, adjustable dumbbells and compact strength equipment.

2026 growth opportunities increasingly come from commercial-grade connected hardware, strength-training products, recovery equipment and refurbishments by gyms, studios, hotels and multifamily properties.

cost_structure.materials_and_components: 2022-2026 largest cost bucket: steel, aluminum, plastics, rubber, motors, electronics, touchscreens, sensors, upholstery and imported subassemblies.
cost_structure.labor: 2022 wages were $341 million, equal to about 16.4% of 2022 revenue, with US plants concentrated in higher-value assembly, machining, fabrication, engineering and quality control.
cost_structure.freight_and_logistics: 2025-2026 costs remain material because treadmills, bikes, racks and weight systems are bulky, heavy and often imported or assembled from imported parts.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 profit was $162 million, or 7.8% of revenue; 2025-2026 margins are helped by lower freight costs versus 2021-2022 and hurt by price competition from imports.
cost_structure.sales_service_and_warranty: 2025-2026 commercial manufacturers carry meaningful costs for dealer networks, installation, maintenance, software support and warranty reserves.

current_dynamics: 2025-2026 commercial demand is firmer than home-fitness demand because gyms, studios and clubs are adding members and reinvesting in facilities after the 2020-2022 disruption.
2025 US manufacturers still face a structural import gap: the 2022 baseline showed $6.099 billion of imports versus $2.082 billion of domestic manufacturing revenue.
2025 connected equipment is shifting from pandemic-era home bikes and treadmills toward commercial platforms, operator software, shared logins and content partnerships.
2025 strength training, functional training and recovery are taking share from traditional home cardio equipment as gyms rebalance floors around member usage.
2026 tariff, freight and sourcing uncertainty keeps pressure on landed costs for import-heavy equipment categories under HTS 9506.91.00.
whats_growing: 2024-2025 US gym membership and visits, with HFA reporting 77 million members in 2024 and 81 million members in 2025.
2025 commercial facility reinvestment, supported by 2024 median facility revenue growth of 9.9% in HFA benchmarking.
2026 connected commercial equipment, including Peloton Commercial Series products scheduled to begin shipping in late 2026.
2025-2026 strength systems, racks, benches, free weights, Pilates and functional-training equipment as operators allocate more floor space to strength and group training.
2025-2026 digital facility-management integrations, preventive maintenance, service contracts and equipment utilization analytics.
whats_shrinking: 2025 home connected-fitness hardware demand, with Peloton connected fitness product revenue down from $991.7 million in FY2024 to $817.1 million in FY2025.
2025 low-margin domestic production of commodity cardio and weight equipment because imported products still dominate US demand.
2024-2025 standalone home-fitness brands weakened by post-pandemic overcapacity, highlighted by BowFlex's 2024 bankruptcy sale.
2025-2026 purely analog cardio differentiation, as buyers increasingly expect screens, apps, diagnostics, content or facility software compatibility.

2026-04-09: HFA reported 81 million US fitness facility members in 2025, up 5.2% from 2024, and more than 100 million total facility users.
2026-08-06: Peloton reported FY2026 Q4 revenue of $607.7 million and guided FY2027 revenue to $2.3-$2.4 billion, signaling continued pressure in connected home fitness.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive for US manufacturing revenue but not for domestic share. The 2022 baseline projection of roughly 2.5% annual growth points to about $2.30 billion of US manufacturing revenue in 2026 and roughly $2.4 billion by 2028, supported by commercial replacement cycles, rising gym visits, strength-training demand and connected commercial launches. Imports will remain the main competitive ceiling, and manufacturers with defensible US operations will likely focus on premium commercial equipment, rapid service, customization, institutional contracts and software-enabled products rather than commodity home cardio. Home-fitness hardware is likely to stay softer through 2026 unless new products, lower price points or subscription bundles revive demand.

title: Gym & Fitness Franchises
one_liner: Franchised gyms and boutique fitness studios are benefiting from renewed in-person workout traffic, but growth is splitting between low-price, high-volume clubs and specialized premium wellness formats.
overview: Gym and fitness franchises sit inside the broader US fitness facility market, which recorded $43.3 billion in 2025 revenue for gyms, health and fitness clubs. The narrow franchised gym-and-studio segment is smaller but influential because major chains such as Planet Fitness, Anytime Fitness, Orangetheory Fitness, Club Pilates, Crunch Fitness, Pure Barre, HOTWORX and F45 use franchising to scale units, buying power, local marketing, and standardized technology. The industry has moved past the 2020 closure shock: 2025 commercial fitness visitation rose 4.2% year over year, high-value low-price gyms rose 4.5%, and operators reported strong 2024 median revenue growth of 9.9%. Demand is now bifurcated, with price-sensitive Gen Z and mass-market consumers favoring low monthly dues, while higher-income consumers pay for Pilates, assisted stretching, recovery, body-composition, coaching, and other measurable wellness formats.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: estimated $4.4 billion US gym and fitness franchise operator revenue, using the baseline IBISWorld 2025 forecast adjusted for 2024-2025 post-pandemic visitation, membership, and pricing gains; broader US gyms, health and fitness clubs revenue was $43.3 billion in 2025.
key_stats.growth: 2025: estimated +7% to +9% revenue growth for franchised gym and fitness operators; HFA reported 2025 visits per location up 4.2% and HVLP visits up 4.5%, while its 2025 benchmarking report showed 2024 median facility revenue growth of 9.9%.
key_stats.establishments: 2026: roughly 36,000 for-profit US fitness facilities; the 10 largest chains operated 10,901 US sites, or 30.3% of the site universe.
key_stats.membership_indicator: 2025: Planet Fitness ended the year with about 20.8 million members and 2,896 global clubs, about 90% independently owned and operated.
key_stats.profitability_indicator: 2025 HFA Benchmarking Report: reporting operators posted a 2024 median EBITDA margin of 23.6%.
key_stats.franchise_wellness_output: 2026: IFA/FRANdata expected franchised health and wellness output to reach $66.4 billion and establishments to exceed 99,000 units.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $3.16 billion implied baseline from the provided IBISWorld 2020 file, calculated from 2020 revenue of $3.009 billion and the report's 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 2.5%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: +2.5% implied forecast growth on the IBISWorld baseline path.
baseline_2022.establishments: 2022: about 8,940 implied establishments on the provided IBISWorld forecast path from 8,575 locations in 2020 to 9,512 in 2025.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022: about 8.3% implied EBIT margin on the IBISWorld baseline path between 8.1% in 2020 and 8.6% forecast for 2025.

how_it_makes_money: Operators primarily sell recurring monthly memberships and annual fees, supplemented by enrollment fees, class packs, personal training, small-group training, guest passes, merchandise, drinks, nutrition products, recovery services, tanning, hydro-massage, sauna, and other add-ons. Franchisees pay royalties, marketing fund contributions, technology fees, training fees, and sometimes required equipment purchases to franchisors; franchisors earn royalties, franchise fees, brand fund revenue, equipment revenue, and support-service revenue.
cost_structure: Major franchisee costs are rent and occupancy, labor for front-desk staff, coaches and trainers, equipment leasing or replacement, utilities, insurance, payment processing, local marketing, cleaning and maintenance, royalties, brand fund fees, software, and debt service. HVLP gyms reduce labor through 24-hour access, EFT billing, standardized layouts, and high member-to-staff ratios, while boutique studios carry higher instructor payroll and customer-acquisition costs but can command premium pricing per class or membership.
current_dynamics: The industry is no longer defined by pandemic recovery alone. In 2025-2026, gym traffic and memberships are growing, but the strongest concepts are those with a clear value proposition: low-cost scale, convenient 24-hour access, boutique community, Pilates and strength training, recovery, or measurable health outcomes. Franchisees still face high build-out costs, higher wages, elevated local ad spending, and more disciplined lending than the pre-2020 period, so franchisors are emphasizing smaller formats, multi-unit operators, shared services, app-based engagement, and technology that improves retention. Large chains continue to gain share by site count and marketing reach, but the US market remains fragmented because about 70% of for-profit fitness sites are independent or small regional operators.
whats_growing: HVLP gyms, strength equipment, Pilates, assisted stretching, recovery and sauna concepts, app-linked coaching, wearable-driven workouts, suburban and secondary-market expansion, multi-unit franchise ownership, corporate wellness partnerships, and add-on revenue streams such as personal training, recovery, and retail products.
whats_shrinking: Undifferentiated mid-priced gyms, undercapitalized boutique concepts with high acquisition costs, formats dependent on one narrow modality without strong retention, pandemic-era digital-only substitution, and older locations that cannot fund equipment refreshes, strength-area expansion, or required brand remodels.
recent_developments: 2025-01: Planet Fitness promoted a $1 down and $15 per month offer for new members, reinforcing HVLP pricing pressure in franchised fitness.
2025-07-28: Xponential Fitness completed the divestiture of CycleBar and Rumble to Extraordinary Brands to focus on higher-priority brands and franchisee profitability.
2025-09-30: HFA released its 2025 Fitness Industry Benchmarking Report, showing 2024 median revenue growth of 9.9% and median EBITDA margin of 23.6% among reporting operators.
2026-01-12: Planet Fitness reported 2025 year-end metrics of 20.8 million members, 6.7% system-wide same-club sales growth, and 181 new club openings.
2026-02: HFA reported that 2025 gym and studio visits per location rose 4.2% year over year, with HVLP gyms up 4.5%.
2026-05-15: IFA/FRANdata said franchised health and wellness establishments were expected to exceed 99,000 in 2026 with 2.1% unit growth and $66.4 billion in output.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but selective. Franchised fitness should grow faster than the old 2020 baseline because in-person visitation, price increases, and wellness add-ons are stronger than expected, while broader discretionary pressure limits weaker operators. The best-positioned franchise systems will be low-price gyms with national scale, boutique brands with high visit frequency and clear modality leadership, and wellness hybrids that layer recovery, coaching, and medical-adjacent services onto recurring memberships. Risks include high rent and construction costs, local labor shortages, franchisee debt service, saturation in top urban markets, and continued competition from independent studios, corporate-owned clubs, and at-home fitness apps.
themes: Boutique fitness shifts toward Pilates, recovery, and measurable outcomes
Franchisees need stronger unit economics and multi-unit scale
Technology, AI, apps, and wearables are retention tools
Fitness is converging with preventive health and wellness
Suburban and secondary markets are more attractive than saturated urban cores
